title: Two Sum · Complement Hash Map
idea: Remember earlier values so each new number can ask whether its missing partner has already appeared.
steps: Compute target minus the current value.
Look for that complement among earlier indices.
If found, return the two different indices. Otherwise remember this value.
Return an empty list if no pair exists.
example: For [2,7,11,15] and target 9, 2 needs 7; at index 1, earlier 2 completes the pair [0,1].
use: Pair lookup and replacing a quadratic nested scan.
watch: nums: up to 20 integers in −100…100; target: −200…200. Returns the first discovered valid index pair. Map space O(n).

title: Three Sum · Unique Triplets
idea: Sort the values, fix one number, and move two pointers to find the remaining pair summing to its opposite.
steps: Sort a copy of the input.
Fix each distinct first value and place pointers at the ends of the remaining suffix.
Move left rightward if the sum is too small; move right leftward if too large.
Record zero-sum triples and skip equal pointer values so each value triple appears once.
example: [-1,0,1,2,-1,-4] gives [-1,-1,2] and [-1,0,1]. These are value triples, not original indices.
use: Finding all distinct zero-sum triples.
watch: nums: up to 20 integers. Target is fixed at 0. Sorting a copy uses O(n) storage in this demo, plus output.

title: Product Except Self · Prefix/Suffix
idea: At each position, multiply everything before it by everything after it, without dividing.
steps: Walk left to right, storing the product strictly before each index.
Walk right to left with a running product strictly after each index.
Multiply the two contributions at that index.
Keep zeros as ordinary factors; division is never needed.
use: Computing per-position aggregates while excluding the current element.
watch: nums: up to 20 integers. Exact-safe-integer overflow is rejected; reduce magnitudes if needed. O(1) running state beyond O(n) output, excluding copied input and traces.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
idea: A subarray has sum k when two prefix totals differ by k. Count how many earlier totals complete that difference.
steps: Start the prefix-frequency map with total 0 occurring once.
Add the current value to the running total.
Add the frequency of current total minus target to the answer.
Only then record the new total for later positions.
example: For [1,1,1] and target 2, the pairs of adjacent ones give two subarrays. Negative values also work.
use: Counting contiguous target-sum ranges, including with negative numbers.
watch: nums: up to 20 integers; target: −200…200. Counts position-distinct nonempty subarrays. O(n) map storage.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
idea: Only start counting a consecutive run at a value that has no predecessor in the set.
steps: Put distinct values in a hash set.
Skip x if x−1 is present: it lies inside an earlier run.
From a run start, count x, x+1, and later present values.
Keep the largest run length; original array order does not matter.
example: [20,4,50,1,3,2] contains the run 1,2,3,4, so the answer is 4.
use: Recognizing runs in unsorted data without sorting.
watch: nums: up to 20 integers. Duplicate values count once. Expected O(n) set storage and total membership work.

title: Trapping Rain Water · Two Pointers
idea: Water over a bar is limited by surrounding walls. Finalize the side whose current boundary is lower.
steps: Place pointers at both ends and track the highest wall seen from each side.
Process the lower boundary side: the opposite side already provides enough support.
Water there is that side’s maximum minus the bar height.
Move inward and accumulate the volume.
example: [3,0,2,0,4] holds 7 units: 3 above the first dip, 1 above height 2, and 3 above the next dip.
use: Computing water trapped between unit-width bars.
watch: nums: nonnegative integer heights, at most 20. Returns volume, not the maximum container area. O(1) core state; the demo also records per-index water.

title: Container With Most Water
idea: Choose two vertical lines maximizing width times the shorter line. Move the shorter side to seek an improvement.
steps: Begin with the widest pair of lines.
Compute width multiplied by the lower height.
Move the pointer at the shorter line; keeping it cannot improve area at a smaller width.
Repeat and remember the maximum.
example: For [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7], lines at indices 1 and 8 give width 7 × height 7 = 49.
use: Proving that a pointer move discards only dominated candidates.
watch: nums: up to 20 nonnegative heights. Fewer than two lines give area 0. O(1) algorithm working state.

title: Dutch National Flag · Three-Way Partition
idea: Keep separate regions for 0s, 1s, unknown values, and 2s, and inspect each unknown value.
steps: low marks the next 0 position, mid the current unknown value, and high the last unknown position.
For 0, swap into low and advance low and mid.
For 1, advance mid.
For 2, swap with high and reduce high; inspect the incoming value before moving mid.
example: [2,0,2,1,1,0] becomes [0,0,1,1,2,2] without a comparison sort.
use: Sorting three categories and building duplicate-aware quickselect partitions.
watch: nums may contain only 0, 1, and 2. O(1) in-place core space; the lesson copies input for replay. Not stable.

title: Search Rotated Sorted Array
idea: A rotation breaks global order, but at least one half around the middle is still sorted.
steps: Compare the middle value with the target.
Determine which half is sorted by comparing its endpoints.
Keep the sorted half only if its value range contains the target; otherwise choose the other half.
Return its original rotated-array index or −1.
example: In [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target 0 is at index 4. The array is not sorted again before searching.
use: Searching a sorted sequence after a cyclic rotation.
watch: nums must be a rotation of distinct increasing integers; up to 20. Search is O(log n); the demo’s upfront validation scans O(n). O(1) search space.

title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
idea: After sorting by start, only the last merged interval can overlap the next one.
steps: Sort intervals by start, then end.
If the next start is no greater than the current merged end, extend the end to their maximum.
Otherwise begin a new merged interval.
Keep the growing list of disjoint intervals.
example: [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10]] merges into [[1,6],[8,10]]. Touching endpoints also merge.
use: Consolidating occupied ranges and simplifying later interval queries.
watch: intervals: up to 16 [start,end] pairs with integer endpoints −100…100 and start < end. Uses closed/touching merge semantics. O(n) output/copy storage.

title: Meeting Rooms II · End-Time Heap
idea: Reuse a room as soon as its earliest-ending meeting finishes; peak simultaneous meetings determine room demand.
steps: Sort meetings by start time.
Remove every active end time no later than the next start.
Add the new meeting end to a min heap.
Record the largest number of active meetings.
example: [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]] needs 2 rooms. A meeting ending at 10 can share a room with one starting at 10.
use: Resource allocation and maximum overlap in time intervals.
watch: Uses half-open [start,end) meetings, unlike the touching-merge lesson. At most 16 intervals, start < end. O(n) heap storage.

title: Top K Frequent Elements · Bounded Heap
idea: Count frequencies, then keep only the best k candidates in a heap whose root is the least desirable retained candidate.
steps: Count each distinct value.
Push a value with its count into the bounded heap.
If there are more than k candidates, remove the worst one.
Sort retained results by decreasing count and then increasing value.
example: [1,1,1,2,2,3] with k=2 returns [1,2]. Equal frequencies prefer smaller numeric values.
use: Finding frequent items when k is smaller than the number of distinct values u.
watch: k ranges from 0 to the number of distinct values. O(u+k) storage; final output ordering adds O(k log k).

title: Kth Largest · Three-Way Quickselect
idea: Partition around a pivot and continue only in the region containing sorted index n−k.
steps: Choose the midpoint value as a deterministic pivot.
Partition into values less than, equal to, and greater than the pivot.
Discard the regions that cannot contain index n−k.
If the index lies in the equal region, return its value.
example: For [3,2,1,5,6,4] and k=2, the second largest value is 5. Duplicate values count as separate positions.
use: Selection without fully sorting every region.
watch: 1 ≤ k ≤ nums.length. Midpoint pivots are deterministic: balanced partitions give O(n), but worst-case time is O(n²). O(1) iterative core state beyond the copied array.

title: Next Greater Element · Monotonic Stack
idea: Keep unresolved indices on a stack until a larger value arrives to answer them.
steps: Scan values from left to right.
Pop every pending index with a strictly smaller value and assign the current value to it.
Push the current index as unresolved.
Indices left on the stack have no greater value to their right.
example: [2,1,2,4,3] produces [4,2,4,-1,-1]. Equal 2s do not answer one another.
use: Next-greater relationships and amortized stack analysis.
watch: Returns values, not indices; −1 denotes absence and can also be a valid answer value. O(n) stack and output space.

title: Sliding Window Maximum · Deque
idea: Discard expired and dominated candidates so the front always identifies the largest value in the current window.
steps: Remove front indices outside the current k-wide window.
Remove back indices whose values are no greater than the arriving value.
Append the arriving index.
Once the window is full, record the value at the deque front.
use: Fast aggregate queries over a moving fixed-size window.
watch: For nonempty nums, 1 ≤ k ≤ n. Empty nums requires k=0 and returns []. Active deque is O(k); this trace uses an array plus a head index and output storage.

title: Jump Game · Reachable Frontier
idea: Track the farthest reachable index instead of trying every jump sequence.
steps: Start with frontier 0.
If the next index lies beyond the frontier, it cannot be reached.
Otherwise extend the frontier with index plus its jump allowance.
Succeed as soon as the final index is covered.
example: [2,3,1,1,4] is reachable; [3,2,1,0,4] is blocked by the zero at index 3.
use: Replacing exponential reachability exploration with a greedy invariant.
watch: nums: nonnegative maximum forward jump lengths. You may jump fewer steps. Empty input returns false; a single reachable starting cell returns true. O(1) state.

title: Gas Station · Circular Greedy
idea: If a route segment fails, none of its possible starting stations can rescue it; move the candidate past that segment.
steps: Track total gas minus cost across the whole circle.
Track the tank balance since the current candidate start.
If that balance goes negative, discard starts through this station and reset after it.
If total balance is nonnegative, the remaining candidate works.
example: gas [1,2,3,4,5] and cost [3,4,5,1,2] yield start index 3.
use: Proving a greedy elimination rule over circular sequences.
watch: gas and cost are equally sized nonnegative arrays, at most 20. Unlimited tank, empty at the chosen start. Empty or infeasible input returns −1. O(1) state.

title: House Robber · Rolling DP
idea: At each house, either skip it or take it together with the best reward ending before its neighbor.
steps: Start with reward 0 for empty prefixes.
Compare previous best with best two houses back plus this house’s value.
Keep the better option and roll the two states forward.
Return the best reward; choosing no house is allowed.
example: [2,7,9,3,1] yields 12 by taking values 2,9,1. Adjacent houses cannot both be selected.
use: Selection problems with local incompatibility constraints.
watch: nums: up to 20 integer rewards, including negatives. Empty or all-negative inputs can yield 0. O(1) core working space; the trace displays prefix results.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
idea: Equal partition is possible exactly when some subset reaches half the total.
steps: Reject an odd total.
Mark sum 0 reachable.
For each value, update possible sums downward so it is used at most once.
Check whether half the total is reachable.
example: [1,5,11,5] can split into [11] and [1,5,5], both totaling 11.
use: 0/1 subset-sum reachability and avoiding accidental item reuse.
watch: nums: nonnegative integers with total ≤ 200. Empty subsets are allowed, so empty input is true. O(sum) DP storage.

title: 0/1 Knapsack · Capacity DP
idea: Choose each item at most once, maximizing value without exceeding the weight capacity.
steps: Initialize best value at every capacity to 0.
For each item, iterate capacities from largest down to its weight.
Compare skipping with taking its value plus the smaller-capacity answer.
Return the best value at the requested capacity.
example: Weights [2,3,4,5], values [3,4,5,6], capacity 5 gives 7 by taking the first two items.
use: Budget-constrained 0/1 choices and pseudo-polynomial DP.
watch: Up to 16 items; weights 0…40, values 0…100, capacity 0…40. Each zero-weight item is still used only once. O(capacity) algorithm space.

title: Subsets · Backtracking
idea: Build every subset by choosing only indices after the last selected one.
steps: Record the current partial selection as a valid subset.
Choose each later index in turn.
Recurse starting after that chosen index.
Undo the choice before exploring the next branch.
example: [1,2] produces [], [1], [1,2], and [2]. The empty subset is included.
use: Generating a power set while maintaining increasing chosen indices.
watch: nums: at most 10 distinct integers. O(n) recursion/path state, excluding exponential output and snapshots.

title: Permutations · Choose/Undo
idea: Choose an unused value for the next position, then undo that choice to explore alternatives.
steps: Track which input indices are currently used.
Append each unused value to the path.
When the path contains every value, record a complete ordering.
Restore the used flag and path after returning.
example: [1,2] gives [1,2] and [2,1]. Unlike subsets, ordering changes the answer.
use: Exploring arrangements with explicit reversible state.
watch: nums: at most 6 distinct integers. Empty input has one empty permutation. O(n) path/used/recursion state, excluding output.

title: Combination Sum · Reusable Choices
idea: Use positive candidates any number of times, but keep choices nondecreasing so different orders do not duplicate a combination.
steps: Deduplicate and sort candidate values.
Try a candidate only if it fits the remaining target.
Recurse from the same candidate index to allow reuse.
Record remaining target 0, then undo choices.
example: Candidates [2,3,6,7], target 7 produce [2,2,3] and [7], not their permutations.
use: Backtracking with reuse, pruning, and canonical output order.
watch: Positive candidates only; target 0…24. Target 0 yields one empty combination. Depth ≤ target/minCandidate; very large traces ask for smaller input.

title: N-Queens · Constraint Backtracking
idea: Place one queen per row, rejecting columns and diagonals already attacked.
steps: Try a safe column in the current row.
Mark its column and the two diagonal identifiers row−column and row+column.
Recurse to the next row.
Record complete boards and undo every mark when backtracking.
example: n=4 has two solution boards. n=2 and n=3 have no solutions.
use: Constraint propagation and undoing state consistently.
watch: n: integer 1…8. Returns all boards as strings; rotations/reflections count separately. O(n) constraint state plus O(n²) displayed board and output.

title: Number of Islands · Grid BFS
idea: Each unseen land cell starts one island; flood its four-directional neighbors before continuing the scan.
steps: Scan every cell.
On an undiscovered 1, increment the island count and enqueue it.
Mark land when enqueuing so it cannot enter the queue twice.
Visit up, down, left, and right until that island is fully labeled.
example: [[1,0],[0,1]] has two islands because diagonal contact does not connect them.
use: Connected components in grids and safe BFS discovery rules.
watch: Rectangular numeric 0/1 grid, at most 8×8. Empty grids give 0. A copied grid uses labels 2 and above for found islands; original input is preserved. O(rows × columns) space.

title: Union–Find · Connected Components
idea: Keep a parent forest describing components and merge roots only when a new edge joins different groups.
steps: Start every vertex in its own group.
Find each endpoint’s root, compressing parent paths.
Attach the smaller root tree to the larger one.
Reduce the component count only when two distinct roots merge.
example: With vertices 0…5 and edges 0–1,1–2,3–4,2–4, vertices 0…4 connect while 5 remains separate: count 2.
use: Incremental undirected connectivity and component grouping.
watch: n: 1…12; up to 24 edges with endpoints 0…n−1. Duplicate edges/self-loops do not reduce the count. O(n) parent/size storage.

title: Fenwick Tree · Updates & Range Sums
idea: Store overlapping partial sums so point additions and prefix queries touch only logarithmically many tree entries.
steps: Build the 1-based tree using point additions.
For each [index,delta], add delta to that value and update ancestors with i += i & −i.
For a prefix, move backward with i -= i & −i.
Inclusive range [l,r] is prefix(r+1) minus prefix(l).
example: [2,1,3,4,5] updated by +2 at index 1 becomes [2,3,3,4,5]. Query sums [0,2] and [1,4] are 8 and 15.
use: Dynamic additive sums when a static prefix array would require costly repairs.
watch: At most 16 values, 8 updates and 8 queries. All updates happen before queries. Public indices are 0-based; tree index 0 is unused. O(n) storage.
